newsitem.title: GERMANY: AMD, Cyrix ready for run at Intel.
newsitem.headline: AMD, Cyrix ready for run at Intel.

text.p: Computer chip makers Advanced Micro Devices Inc and Cyrix Corp think Intel Corp's dominance of their industry is finally about to end.

After past attempts to catch Intel left them in the red, both AMD and Cyrix demonstrated next-generation computer chips at the CeBIT trade fair that they are counting on to spark rebounds and match their arch rival in processing power.
Even though Intel is about to unleash a new chip family of its own -- the Pentium II -- Cyrix and AMD both said they have learned from the mistakes that dashed their assaults on Intel two years ago.

"We didn't really know how to market against Pentium back then and we had manufacturing glitches for two quarters," Steve Tobak, Cyrix vice president of marketing, told Reuters. "I definitely think this is the year of the alternative processor."

AMD has ironed out production problems that fouled up the launch of its K5 processor in 1995, said Dirk Heinen, a product manager for AMD's forthcoming chip, the K6. "We are doing a lot of things better this time around," he said.
The K6, which should appear in PCs this summer, was shown at CeBIT running at 200 megahertz, a speed that would put it in a class with Intel's top performer, the 200 megahertz Pentium Pro.
The K6 is a critical product for AMD, which has just returned to profitability after the K5 delay caused sales to drop sharply.

Cyrix should also return to the black this year now that it has clear up problems with its last chip, the 6x86, Tobak said. At CeBIT, Cyrix reached 166 megahertz with its next-generation M2 processor, which should be ready in the fall.
When it's ready, the M2 would run at faster speeds, but Cyrix planned to sell it for the same price as Pentium chips with slower clock speeds, Tobak said.
"We understand now that we can't position it against the top of Intel's line," he said. "We are going to position it aggressively against the mid-range Pentiums."
Both the K6 and M2 have the MMX multimedia capability that Intel added to its Pentium line in January.
But even if Cyrix offers more speed at a lower price, the Richardson, Texas, company has to work hard to convince PC makers to leave Intel, he admitted. "We've got a big challenge."
In the mean time, Intel is not sitting still. It's Pentium II chip, due in May or June, would run at speeds "well above 200 megahertz," Intel desktop products chief Pat Gelsinger said.

Last month Intel demonstrated a Pentium II chip running at 400 megahertz under special conditions. "Over the long haul, the (Penitum II) family can clearly scale up to those speeds," Intel marketing manager Tim Miller told Reuters at CeBIT.
Moreover, Intel is able to deliver chips in such volume that PC makers like Dell Computer Corp. or Hewlett Packard Co. can begin selling computers as soon as Intel has the chip ready.
AMD and Cyrix require several weeks to get up to speed.
Tobak said several small PC makers who don't require big volumes of chips were very interested in the M2.
Heinen declined to name PC companies planning to use the chip, but said a group of German companies that have signed up would make an announcement April 4.
"Most of them are companies that do a lot of business in the consumer space," he told Reuters. "K6 will do well there."

He also said four of the world's top ten PC makers are seriously interested in K6. "They might not use it right out the the chute, but we think our chances are pretty good for later this year," he said.
